The bathtub curve

How failure rates vary throughout an asset’s lifespan: and how to use that data to guide maintenance choices.

Prashant Dhingra · 17-slide guide

Explore the slidesRead the FAQ
OverviewThe curveApplications & evidenceData to decisionsAI & metricsFAQ
The central idea

Different failure mechanisms need different responses.

The bathtub curve represents a conceptual failure hazard pattern: it declines early in a product’s life, remains roughly steady during a middle phase, and rises again as wear-out mechanisms develop. It serves as a helpful hypothesis for assessment: not a universal lifecycle applicable to all machines.

This guide follows the provided slides, detailing the mathematics, evidence, pump example, and connections to predictive maintenance. The original images remain intact, with added explanations in the text regarding hazard, confidence intervals, and competing risks.

Rate, not probability: Hazard represents the immediate failure rate for those still surviving. Over a brief time period Δt, the conditional probability of failure is roughly h(t)Δt.

The three phases at a glance

PatternWeibull shapeQuestions for maintenance
Decreasing hazardβ < 1Are defects, installation or repairs driving early failures?
Constant hazardβ = 1Can monitoring, redundancy or spares reduce consequences?
Increasing hazardβ > 1Does planned intervention outperform waiting or monitoring?

These β values correspond to a fitted two-parameter Weibull model. Capturing a complete bathtub curve necessitates a more complex or piecewise model, or a suitable combination of failure mechanisms.

01 / Foundations

Understand the curve and its mathematics

SLIDE 01

The bathtub curve

The bathtub curve illustrates how the failure hazard of an asset population varies over time: initially high risk, followed by a stable middle phase, and finally a rising wear-out risk. It links reliability assessment with maintenance scheduling and predictive AI.

SLIDE 02

From a familiar chart to practical decisions

The deck addresses the curve, hazard and Weibull mathematics, applications, historical evidence, fitting workflows, and maintenance decisions. Its purpose is to evaluate the pattern using asset data instead of presuming it is universally applicable.

SLIDE 03

What the curve actually shows

The vertical axis represents the failure hazard for surviving units, rather than the cumulative failure probability. Early defects can cause a decreasing hazard, random failure mechanisms tend to result in an approximately constant hazard, and degradation leads to an increasing hazard. Not all assets show all three phases.

SLIDE 04

Three phases, three responses

Initial failures highlight the need for improved manufacturing, installation, commissioning, and well-founded screening. Ongoing age-related risk supports consequence-focused monitoring, redundancy, or allowing run-to-failure. Growing hazard levels may warrant planned interventions when justified by economic factors and failure mechanisms.

SLIDE 05

Hazard rate and Weibull shape

The hazard function is h(t) = f(t) / S(t), with S(t) = 1 − F(t). In the case of a two-parameter Weibull, h(t) = (β/η)(t/η)^(β−1): when β is less than one, the hazard decreases; when β equals one, the hazard remains constant; and when β is greater than one, the hazard increases. A single two-parameter Weibull cannot generate the complete bathtub-shaped hazard.

02 / Evidence

Applications, limits and historical patterns

SLIDE 06

Where reliability analysis helps

Applications encompass maintenance selection, screening, warranty reserves, spare parts forecasting, accelerated testing, and replacement planning. Decisions ought to integrate failure-mode data with consequences, uncertainty, and overall cost, rather than depend solely on a single curve or percentile.

SLIDE 07

When to use the model cautiously

Examine similar units and identify failure mechanisms. Infrequent events, variable loads, combined environments, repairs, and interacting factors can mask aging effects. Confirm the model’s accuracy under real operating conditions prior to using its forecasts for a different fleet.

SLIDE 08

Hard-drive evidence is cohort-specific

The deck references Backblaze’s historical 2013 annualized failure rates: 5.1% in the first 18 months, 1.4% between 18 months and three years, and 11.8% from three to four years. These figures represent past fleet data, not current forecasts for individual drives. Subsequent Backblaze analyses reveal that the failure rate patterns vary depending on product type and operating timeframe.

SLIDE 09

Six patterns, not one universal law

The presentation replicates traditional airline reliability patterns along with their historical proportions, including a 4% bathtub category. These percentages pertain specifically to that study context and should not be applied universally to all equipment. Limited age dependence does not diminish the importance of inspections or other maintenance based on consequence.

03 / Decisions

From fleet records to maintenance strategy

SLIDE 10

Match the strategy to the mechanism

To reduce hazard, examine defects and minimize unnecessary intrusive activities. For a constant age hazard, assess condition data, redundancy, and potential consequences. When hazard increases with age, weigh planned replacement against inspection and condition-based maintenance. The age pattern of a failure mode serves as one factor in decision-making, not the whole policy.

SLIDE 11

Build the curve from complete records

Gather exposure time, event status, failure cause, and operating context, including units that remain operational. Divide into suitable cohorts, estimate survival or cumulative hazard, fit potential models, and perform validation. Kaplan–Meier estimates survival; however, estimating instantaneous hazard needs an additional approach rather than directly extracting it from a survival curve.

SLIDE 12

Interpret the fitting example carefully

The slide’s lifelines example applies mode-specific Weibull models to a synthetic pump fleet. Considering other failure modes as censored enables cause-specific hazard analysis within the model’s framework. However, it does not equate 1 − S for the fitted mode to the actual cumulative incidence in the presence of competing risks. A β confidence interval including one indicates that a constant hazard is still consistent with the data, though not conclusively established.

SLIDE 13

Three pump modes and different actions

The illustrative seal estimate indicates a decreasing hazard, while the bearing estimate indicates an increasing hazard; the motor interval, however, does not clarify the direction. With β = 3.09 and η = 17,751 hours, the fitted Weibull B10 is approximately 8,570 hours. This represents a model percentile, not a mandatory replacement time or a competing-risk incidence measure.

04 / Predictive maintenance

AI, misconceptions and reliability metrics

SLIDE 14

Combine reliability statistics with AI

Age, repair history, duty, and sensor data can enhance survival and failure-risk models once their predictive accuracy is confirmed. Models should be calibrated according to failure mechanisms and operational conditions. Generative AI can provide explanations for estimates, but maintenance decisions must stay grounded in engineering evidence and authorized protocols.

SLIDE 15

Common misconceptions

Not all equipment exhibits a bathtub curve, and age by itself does not dictate risk. Intrusive maintenance may cause defects. MTBF and MTTF represent averages rather than specific failure times; MTTF can also be defined for lifetime distributions with nonconstant hazard rates. When multiple failure modes compete, a detailed system model is necessary.

SLIDE 16

Reliability metrics in context

Hazard is an instantaneous rate measured in units of inverse time. In a two-parameter Weibull lifetime model, η represents the 63.2nd percentile of failure, while B10 denotes the 10th percentile. MTBF refers to the intervals between failures in repairable systems, whereas MTTF pertains to the time until failure. AFR is an annualized rate normalized by exposure and is not necessarily the probability that a unit fails within a year.

SLIDE 17

Use the curve as a testable model

Determine the mechanism, retain censored data, measure uncertainty, and choose a maintenance approach based on both risk and impact. Integrate age-related reliability models with verified condition information, and reevaluate assumptions whenever there are changes in the fleet, operating conditions, or repair procedures.

Questions, answered

Bathtub curve FAQ

What is the bathtub curve?

The bathtub curve illustrates how the failure hazard of an asset population varies over time: initially high risk, followed by a stable middle phase, and finally a rising wear-out risk. It links reliability assessment with maintenance scheduling and predictive AI.

What does Weibull beta mean?

In a two-parameter Weibull model, β < 1 indicates decreasing hazard, β = 1 constant hazard, and β > 1 increasing hazard. One such model represents a monotonic phase, not the entire bathtub.

Does every asset follow this pattern?

No. Different failure mechanisms, population makeup, operating conditions, and maintenance history result in varying patterns. Validate the model using similar asset data.

What is B10 life?

B10 represents the time at which the fitted lifetime model estimates that 10% of units have failed. For a two-parameter Weibull distribution, B10 = η[−ln(0.9)]^(1/β). On its own, it does not serve as an ideal replacement interval.

Why include units that have not failed?

The observed operating time offers insights into survival. These are right-censored observations, not missing data; excluding them can lead to biased reliability estimates.

Does a confidence interval that includes beta = 1 demonstrate constant hazard?

No. It indicates that a constant hazard aligns with that estimate and its uncertainty. Further data, diagnostics, and engineering evidence might be required.

Sources and interpretation

Further reading

This page modifies the provided 17-slide “The Bathtub Curve” presentation. Pump results are illustrative examples; the shown Python code has not been executed on an actual fleet dataset. Historical airline proportions are taken from the presentation figures, not from comprehensive asset data.

  • NIST: Weibull Distribution : distribution and hazard formulas.
  • Backblaze: How Long Do Disk Drives Last? : fleet-specific drive reliability context.
  • Backblaze: Revisiting the Bathtub Curve : why historical patterns should be reassessed for newer populations.

Determining maintenance intervals involves analyzing failure consequences, operating conditions, uncertainty, and costs. Relying solely on a fitted B10 value or a single point estimate does not determine the optimal intervention timing.
